questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] percentage experiments with exposure logging and auto-abort on a flag store (organized-study-cal-com, cal.diy/fabledocs/upskill/03-architecture-and-patterns/06-architecture-critique.md). Scenario: product wants to test a new booking-confirmation flow as a real experiment rather than a toggle, ramping it to 5%, then 25%, then 100% of 18,000 teams. Bookings peak at 5,000 a minute; guardrail metrics must be able to abort the experiment automatically, and the abort has to take effect everywhere within 10 minutes. Write your design before you look: how a subject is assigned to an arm so that the assignment is stable through the ramp, who the subject is, how exposure is recorded and at what volume, which guardrails trigger an abort and how fast, and how an abort differs from killing the feature. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Assignment is a deterministic hash, not a stored coin flip: today's flags are booleans with variants left for later, so the arm comes from hash(subject id + experiment slug) mod 1000 compared against a threshold (50, then 250, then 1000); raising the threshold only adds subjects, so a team that was in at 5% is still in at 25%, and every instance computes the same answer with no lookup.

[w3] The subject is the team, not the user: a booking involves an organizer and attendees, and the person on the public booking page often has no session at all (the route substitutes a placeholder id), so a user hash cannot even key them; hashing the team (or the owner of a personal event type) shows both sides of one booking the same flow.

[w2] The schema already lets a flag be typed as an experiment, yet nothing in the evaluation path behaves differently by type, so the experiment needs its own definition: slug, threshold, start time, guardrails and a state of running, frozen or aborted.

[w3] Exposure is one event per subject per experiment, written the first time the experiment is evaluated for that team (team, arm, time); at 5,000 bookings a minute (about 83 a second) deduplication caps it at one row per team, at most 18,000 per experiment, and it goes through the existing typed task queue, which already has an analytics-event task, never as a write on the booking path.

[w2] Flag rows cannot serve as the record of who saw what: the team setter upserts, overwriting the enabled value and the assigner in place with no earlier state kept, so the exposure log is the only history the analysis can trust.

[w3] Guardrails run per arm over a sliding window with a minimum sample: booking errors, confirmation-render failures and completed bookings in the new flow against control, evaluated every minute; the detection window plus the time for the change to reach every instance must fit inside 10 minutes, and an automated abort writes as a named system actor because the flag row records who changed it and when.

[w3] An abort is not a kill: aborting freezes the experiment (threshold to zero, so every team gets control, no new exposures, and existing assignments kept for analysis), while a kill turns the feature off everywhere whatever any experiment says. The repository's team listing does treat a globally disabled flag as off for everyone, but only that listing: the per-team check a booking runs answers from team rows and their parents alone, so the kill has to sit inside evaluation itself, checked before any team answer.
[w1] Each ramp step is a small, reversible change with a test written to fail first, so stepping from 5% to 25% is a reviewed edit to one threshold.
keyPoints.quote: behind flags where behavior changes, with a failing-first test

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the experiment runs at 25% and three things go wrong. A first version bucketed by user, so in one team the organizer saw the new flow while the attendee's confirmation rendered the old one; the guardrail fired and the abort flipped the experiment's database row, yet some instances kept serving the new flow well past the 10-minute promise; and exposure events were written synchronously on the booking path, one insert per booking, until that table became the hottest in the database. What breaks, how does each show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] User bucketing splits shared flows: organizer and attendee hash independently, and an anonymous attendee has no id to hash, so one booking renders two versions; bucket by team and stamp the arm on the booking itself, so every later page and email for that booking uses the recorded arm instead of re-evaluating.

[w3] The abort reached the row but not every copy: any cached value the write path does not explicitly clear lives out its time-to-live, five minutes by default, and detection had already used part of the budget; the abort must clear or bypass every copy (shared keys and in-process caches alike) or the evaluation must read a short-lived experiment state, so detection plus propagation stays inside 10 minutes.

[w3] A synchronous exposure insert adds about 83 writes a second to one table, all landing on the newest index pages, and puts a database write inside every booking's latency; deduplicate per team and hand the event to the queue, accepting a rare lost exposure over a slower booking.
keyPoints.quote: Side effects are off the request path and retried.

keyPoints.text: [w2] The repo's own critique already flags work enqueued after commit rather than inside the transaction, so an exposure can be lost between the commit and the enqueue, and a retried task can log the same one twice; deduplicate on team and experiment, and treat the exposure log as a sample the analysis checks rather than trusts blindly.
keyPoints.quote: Effects enqueued after commit, not in-transaction

keyPoints.text: [w2] Watch the sample ratio: at a 25% threshold roughly a quarter of exposed teams should be in treatment, and a skew means bucketing or logging is broken (for example exposures logged only on success, which hides the very failures the guardrail exists to catch); log at evaluation time, before the outcome is known.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your experiment design against the alternatives: bucketing by user versus by team; a threshold on a hash versus an assignment row per subject; logging every exposure inline versus sampling exposures; and reusing the flag store and its scopes for experiments versus a dedicated assignment service. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Users give far more units and so more statistical power, but split shared flows and cannot cover anonymous bookers; teams keep each booking consistent at the cost of fewer units, and a few huge teams can dominate a metric unless results are weighted or capped per team.

[w3] A hash threshold is stateless, needs no writes and stays stable through the ramp, but there is nothing to inspect and no way to force one team without an override layer; assignment rows are explicit, auditable and forcible, at the cost of thousands of writes per ramp step, and the repository can list the teams with an enabled row, which then is the treatment list.

[w2] Logging every evaluation is exact but scales with bookings; once per team per experiment is exact for first exposure and tiny; sampling evaluations cuts volume further but loses each team's first-exposure time and weakens the sample-ratio check, so it suits only very hot paths.

[w2] Reusing the flag store gives one evaluation path plus existing caching and admin tooling, but its contract answers yes-or-no questions and sets tri-state rows, with nowhere to put arms, thresholds or a frozen state; a dedicated assignment service models those and the exposure log properly, at the cost of another component on the booking path and its own availability story.
[w1] However assignment is done, the ramp is a sequence of small reversible steps, each with its own guardrail window before the next.
keyPoints.quote: Guardrails: every change small and reversible
